title: Outbound reply rates near zero? Don't blame the copy yet — check who you're sending to first
dek: Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: if the person is wrong, even perfect copy won't land. The YC partner's debugging order is — check the recipient first, then the company, then the subject line, and only then the copy.
why: Eight tactics in 12 minutes — dense, but every one is an action you can take immediately. For founders stuck at single-digit outbound reply rates who don't know what to change.
who: Early founders whose outbound reply rate is near zero and who can't tell whether to fix the copy or the list; and technical founders doing founder-led sales for the first time.
skip: Point 4, LinkedIn profile optimization (7:16-8:20), is basic and can be skipped.

points.h: Send a hundred by hand before you talk about automation
points.body: The most common founder mistake is opening a tool, blasting a thousand emails, and getting zero replies. The real loss isn't the zero replies themselves — it's that you learned nothing from them. The problem could be the copy, the company targeting, the lead filtering, deliverability, or the subject line, and you can't tell which. So before automating, do at least a hundred outbound attempts by hand — genuinely by hand: spend time researching one specific person, what her problem is, what would grab her attention, read her LinkedIn and her company page. That homework is where high-converting outbound ideas come from.

points.h: Picking the right person matters far more than polishing copy
points.body: Founders routinely spend hours rewriting email wording while barely thinking about who they're sending to. Outbound is like finding a needle in a haystack: you have to find the person who has exactly the pain point you solve, or the most carefully polished copy won't land. One winter batch company selling infrastructure products should have been selling to senior engineering leaders, but its actual list was full of dev rel managers, GTM managers, and even customer success managers — it sent hundreds of emails and of course got no replies. Those wrong titles were never going to buy, regardless of how well the email was written.

points.h: Work backwards from closed customers to the target title
points.body: How do you find the right title? Look at your existing customers first, then at the sales process: who pushed the last deal through, who signed the contract, who paid the money — list all their titles and go find people with similar profiles. You can also look at who has replied to your outbound. If you're still at the very earliest stage, with neither customers nor replies, ask yourself: who in the organization benefits most from buying your software. Example: selling employee device security monitoring software, the chief security officer could get fired over a data breach, so he'll be interested; an engineering manager would probably rather not be monitored, so he's not a good target.

points.h: List-building tools will hand you the wrong companies
points.body: Another common mistake is searching in Sales Navigator and getting back a pile of results that look like a match but are the wrong type of company — search tech companies, for instance, and you often get a pile of IT implementation consultancies. So use list-building tools very carefully, and verify company by company whether it's really your customer. After doing enough outbound, you start noticing the clues that a company needs your product — intent signals. Job postings are a great thing to watch, because they reveal a company's priorities; company growth is another common signal: selling compensation planning software, a company under 100 people probably hasn't introduced job levels yet, and one over 500 has probably already set its salary bands, so crossing the 100-person mark is a great signal. Every product has signals like this; your job is to find your own.

points.h: Shake the tree of your personal network for your first customers
points.body: When closing your first few customers, starting from your personal network is much easier and converts at a much higher rate. Really shake the tree — make sure you've covered everyone you know: your personal network first, then ask friends, family, investors, college roommates, people you met at a coffee shop for intros — literally anyone you can think of.

points.h: Executives don't care about your product features
points.body: The single most important thing in the email is clearly stating how you can help the other person. Figure out the three things that keep the buyer up at night: what gets him fired, what gets him promoted, and why he should believe you can help. When buyers read the email and think ‘this is exactly my problem’, they're likely willing to take the call, even if they don't fully understand or trust your solution yet. The fact is executives don't care about your product features, don't care that your upload speed is blazing fast, and don't care that your database is written in rust — what they worry about is hitting their quarterly targets. Keep the product description to one sentence at most, and save the details for the first call.

points.h: A good email reads like a peer wrote it, not like a pitch
points.body: The email from the founder of Aptin, a YC company in the S24 batch, is held up as an example: the tone is very casual, it sounds like a peer, it uses no jargon, it doesn't try to look impressive, it reads like something a friend sent. He builds credibility with the first line — ‘I used to be a software engineer at Tesla. We got crazy good at using SMS to convert the people who visited our website into car buyers.’ The ending has a very clear call to action: would you be open to running an experiment to see whether AI can reactivate leads and lift conversion. The email also mentions that he noticed the phone number collected in the signup flow on their website, which makes it feel personalized; and the whole thing barely explains how the product works — it only talks about how to help the other person solve their problem.

points.h: On LinkedIn, mutual connections are the number one predictor
points.body: If email is about the subject line, LinkedIn is about your profile — it determines whether people accept your connection request and whether they reply. Key points: having a photo boosts trust; turn the top banner into an ad for your company that states clearly and concisely what the company does, avoiding jargon; rewrite your one-line headline and your about section into a short company description; move up what buyers care about (relevant and impressive experience, say) and cut what's irrelevant — if the about section is a long list of hobbies and interests, it's harder for buyers to see how you can help them. Another place worth investing in is mutual connections: the number of shared connections is the single biggest predictor of whether someone accepts a connection request, so accumulate relevant mutual connections with your target audience — it takes time, and you should turn it into a habit of using your full connection quota every day.

points.h: When reply rates are low, debug in this six-step order
points.body: Reply rates can be very low at first, and that's fine — as long as a few replies come in, you have a baseline to iterate on: 2 to 3 replies out of 100 emails is a great starting point. The debugging order is: first, confirm you're contacting the right people; second, confirm you're contacting the right companies; third, confirm the subject line is good; then, and only then, actually start looking at the copy; after that, look at your materials, such as whether your website and LinkedIn profile look decent; and only last, look at deliverability. If all six of these are reasonable and you still get zero replies, that often may indicate a deeper product-market fit problem.

points.h: Follow up until they say no, then move like a heat-seeking missile
points.body: Don't send just one email — the other person probably just missed it. Usually follow up two to four times, a few days apart. The last email to a prospect is often a breakup message, along the lines of: since I haven't heard back, it looks like sales tax automation isn't a priority for you right now, just let me know and I'll stop cluttering your inbox. This one often gets a reply, because the pressure on the other person to say ‘no’ is very low. A real ‘no’ is actually useful: a large number of ‘nos’ improves your future targeting. Once you get a reply, move like a heat-seeking missile — nothing should stand between you and getting him on the calendar. Every founder goes through the painful lesson of ‘time kills deals’ at least once.

points.h: The best copy comes from customers' own words
points.body: The best feedback on copy always comes from customers — not friends, not advisors, and not your co-founder. Two methods: one, on sales calls ask ‘what made you notice my message’; they'll usually point out which sentences in the email were most interesting, and you should use those sentences in future messages — the question also gets them talking openly about their problem, which is exactly what you want on a first call. Two, ask existing customers how they think about your product, ask what the one thing was that made them decide to buy, and then write future messages in their wording. Customers always write better copy than you do.
